overview.text: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the most advanced stage of infection with HIV, the virus that causes HIV infection; the terms are related but not interchangeable. HIV damages CD4 immune cells, weakening the body’s ability to fight infections and some cancers. In the United States, an AIDS diagnosis is made when a person’s CD4 count falls below 200 cells per cubic millimeter of blood or when certain AIDS-defining illnesses occur. Without effective treatment, HIV may progress to AIDS, sometimes after years. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can prevent or slow that progression and help the immune system recover. An AIDS diagnosis signals severe immune damage, but treatment can still help.

key_facts.text: AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
HIV is the virus; AIDS is an advanced stage of HIV infection, not a separate virus.
CD4 cells help the immune system fight infections; HIV attacks and destroys these cells.
In the United States, either a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or certain illnesses can qualify someone for an AIDS diagnosis.
ART does not cure HIV, but it can control the virus and help prevent progression to AIDS.
